claim: On Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) Competition III dataset IVa (5 subjects, 118 channels, right hand versus foot imagery), sparse common spatial pattern (SCSP) selection averaged 82.28% test accuracy with 22.6 channels, against 73.56% with all 118 channels and 69.28% with C3, C4 and Cz only; a sparser setting kept 79.28% with 7.6 channels.

Fig. 6 (log axis) shows accuracy rising from 3 to about 10 selected channels and drifting down towards 118. claim: Counterpoint on noise: Grover and Venkatesh argue that the useful sensor count is set by the spatial frequency at which signal power meets the noise floor; white sensor noise sets such a cutoff, but if brain noise (filtered by the head like the signal) dominates, the count at which localization stops improving could be quite high.

source.authors: Grover P, Venkatesh P
source.title: An Information-Theoretic View of EEG Sensing

quote: with “brain-noise” as the dominant noise source, the limiting number of sensors at which improvements in localization accuracy saturate could be quite high
notes: Conceptual figure, not data. It cuts against a simple rule that extra electrodes stop helping once sensor noise is below the brain background: in their model a brain-noise floor with a signal-like spatial spectrum imposes no sharp cutoff by itself, while the white sensor-noise floor does. Their Fig. 11 shows a deep brain-noise source mainly hurts localization of deep sources, while a shallow one causes large errors. Preprint wording.

claim: Of the electroencephalography (EEG) noise terms (sensor circuitry, residual artifacts, external interference, and brain activity unrelated to the task), the brain-generated term is described as the hardest to reduce.

source.authors: Grover P, Venkatesh P
source.title: An Information-Theoretic View of EEG Sensing

evidence_location: Section III-C, 'Noise due to a brain source'
quote: The “brain noise” term is probably the most difficult to reduce because estimating it requires solving another inverse problem.
notes: Preprint wording.

claim: An ultra-dense electrode patch revealed strong scalp potential variation at the 1 cm scale and gave twice the signal-to-noise ratio for brain-response classification compared with high-density systems (up to 256 electrodes, 2 to 4 cm apart).

notes: Full text not checked. Robinson et al. 2017 describe the array as 'a small 4 × 4 grid of electrodes'; Ming et al. 2026 describe it as reducing spacing over parieto-occipital scalp from 3 to 1 cm. Local patch, not whole-head coverage.

claim: With up to 512 electrodes 8.6 mm apart over occipital cortex (4 subjects, 4-class visual category decoding, chance 25%), accuracy averaged 73.2% for the full ultra-high-density (uHD) array (464 electrodes used on average), against 69.9% for a 10-05 subset (143.8), 65.5% for extended 10-10 (33.0), 64.0% for 10-10 (25.5) and 57.2% for 10-20 (8.8).

quote: The uHD EEG system consistently outperformed all configurations, achieving the highest average accuracy (73.2%) across subjects
notes: A measured gain beyond 256 electrodes, but over one scalp region and in only 4 subjects (the P values are across cross-validation folds, not subjects). From about 144 to 464 electrodes added 3.3 points; from 8.8 to 25.5 added 6.8 points. Most authors work for g.tec, the system maker.

claim: In the same 512-electrode occipital setup, single-trial regression of image properties averaged Pearson r = 0.50 for the full ultra-high-density (uHD) array against 0.48 (10-05 subset), 0.44 (extended 10-10), 0.43 (10-10) and 0.37 (10-20), with gains continuing below 10 mm spacing.

quote: Our analyses highlight the importance of electrode density with improvements in decoding performance extending even below 10 mm of inter-electrode distance.
notes: Same group and 4 subjects. The step from the 10-05 subset to the full array adds only 0.02 in r.

claim: With 256 ultra-high-density (uHD) channels (8.6 mm spacing) over contralateral sensorimotor cortex, pairwise classification of individual executed finger movements averaged 64.8% (5 subjects, chance 50%).

claim: Background activity can be modelled as randomly distributed cortical dipoles; for isotropic random dipoles in a spherical head the variance of a bipolar (differential) signal depends only on electrode distance, which gives a spatial covariance matrix for background noise in evoked-potential recordings.
